cards.role: Two-colour fixing with a planeswalker bonus
cards.why: Both reviewers value the cycle for reliable access to two colours; a planeswalker can let it enter untapped.
cards.better: Use it when both colours help your mana base, including a supported splash.
cards.watch: Plan early turns assuming it may enter tapped; controlling a planeswalker is a condition, not a guarantee.

cards.name: Ajani Resolute
cards.role: A cheap planeswalker that needs lifegain
cards.why: Other lifegain sources can build loyalty toward a token or an eventual team bonus.
cards.better: Repeated lifegain and creatures that protect it let the low-cost engine develop.
cards.watch: Its own zero ability is slow and it does not immediately protect itself.
cards.disagreement: Quinn doubts the setup is worth it in Limited; Josh sees substantial potential for only two mana.

cards.name: Danitha, Sword of Hope
cards.role: A draw engine with a deck-building requirement
cards.why: Equipment spells and spells targeting your creatures can replace themselves with a card.
cards.better: Enough cheap, useful triggers make it more than a small first-strike creature.
cards.watch: Only one draw per turn is available; a couple of support cards are not a reliable engine.

cards.name: Ghalta the Immovable
cards.role: A toughness payoff with a high starting cost
cards.why: Your largest toughness discounts it and can turn defensive creatures into attackers.
cards.better: Several high-toughness bodies already worth playing make the discount and team effect useful.
cards.watch: Without a substantial creature on board it can remain expensive and stranded in hand.

cards.name: Gideon's Memorial
cards.why: It can improve a token army, or be discarded to deal four damage to an attacking or blocking creature.
cards.better: Multiple token makers make the permanent mode worthwhile.
cards.watch: Its mana only casts planeswalker spells; empower abilities do not qualify, and the removal requires combat.
cards.disagreement: Quinn values the token bonus with a removal fallback; Josh expects the narrow combat-removal mode to be its usual job.

cards.name: Koth of the Homestead
cards.role: Land drops that trigger lifegain and growth
cards.why: Every land gains life, while Plains add a counter to a creature.
cards.better: A white-heavy lifegain deck uses both triggers consistently.
cards.watch: Only Plains give the counter; a green-white dual without the Plains type does not qualify.
cards.disagreement: Quinn mainly wants it in the lifegain archetype; Josh values its independent growth more highly.

cards.name: Liliana the Faultless
cards.role: A cheap lifegain enabler with protection
cards.why: Other creatures and planeswalkers entering supply repeated lifegain triggers.
cards.better: Lifegain payoffs and a valuable permanent worth protecting give it two useful roles.
cards.watch: The protection costs a discarded card, tapping and mana, and cannot target Liliana herself.

cards.name: Lyra, Archangel of Dawn
cards.role: An efficient flyer that grows with lifegain
cards.why: A strong three-mana flying body can quickly become larger with repeated life triggers.
cards.better: Cheap recurring lifegain makes it a major threat without requiring other Angels.
cards.watch: The counters go only on Angels, not your entire team.

cards.name: Rescue Girl, First Responder
cards.role: A flyer for reusing arrival effects
cards.why: Returning your own permanents lets you cast them again for more enters value.
cards.better: Several worthwhile arrival effects justify the mana spent replaying cards.
cards.watch: The ability works only during your turn; it cannot protect against removal on an opponent's turn.

cards.name: Saheeli, Consul of Oversight
cards.role: A flying threat with a token engine
cards.why: Scrying or surveilling adds a Thopter while the main body already pressures the air.
cards.better: Selection effects that fit naturally into your turns make the engine reliable.
cards.watch: The token trigger happens only once each turn, regardless of how many times you scry or surveil.

cards.name: Teyo, Lightshield Expert
cards.role: Protection that leaves a creature behind
cards.why: Flash hexproof can counter targeted interaction while adding a counter and another body.
cards.better: Hold it for a valuable permanent or a combat where the added counter changes the outcome.
cards.watch: Hexproof stops opposing targeting; it does not stop untargeted sweepers or sacrifice effects.

cards.name: Thalia, the Survivor
cards.role: A lifelink creature with a matchup bonus
cards.why: Lifelink helps races, while the tax makes opposing noncreature spells more awkward.
cards.better: Spell-heavy opponents feel the tax most, including when casting prepared noncreature spells.
cards.watch: The tax does little against a creature-heavy draw, so judge the body and lifelink first.

cards.name: Tomik, Orzhov Lawmage
cards.role: Cheap flying pressure with useful support
cards.why: A two-power flyer is a useful baseline, with extra protection for planeswalkers and evasion for counter-bearing creatures.
cards.better: Counters on a large ground creature give the tap ability a worthwhile target.
cards.watch: Tapping Tomik to grant flying means giving up its own attack or block, and the target must already have a counter.

cards.name: Way of the Healer
cards.why: The arrival empower supplies fuel for a token-making loyalty ability and future empower effects keep it going.
cards.better: A protected planeswalker can turn repeated loyalty into a board over several turns.
cards.watch: Each planeswalker normally activates only one loyalty ability per turn; five loyalty does not mean two immediate tokens.
cards.disagreement: Quinn is enthusiastic about the ongoing token engine; Josh places more weight on how slowly its value arrives.

cards.name: Way of the Mentor
cards.why: It supplies initial loyalty and can convert later life triggers into further planeswalker fuel.
cards.better: Frequent lifegain and a protected planeswalker are needed for repeated value.
cards.watch: It adds no new loyalty ability, and accumulating counters does not let one planeswalker activate multiple times in a turn.

cards.name: Yoshimaru, Beloved Companion
cards.why: Each counter-placement event on your creatures adds one extra counter.
cards.better: Several efficient counter sources make the three-mana investment matter.
cards.watch: Its own counter ability costs six and targets a legendary creature; that is a fallback rather than sufficient support.

cards.name: Yuriko, Blade of the Mighty
cards.role: Combat certainty and a lone-attacker payoff
cards.why: A creature attacking a player alone gains double strike while combat spells and most activated abilities are shut off.
cards.better: An evasive or trampling attacker makes double strike more threatening.
cards.watch: The restriction applies to you too: cast needed tricks before combat, and do not count on activated abilities during it.

cards.name: Arni, Humble Scribe
cards.why: Looting improves your hand, and new nontoken creatures can untap it for another use.
cards.better: Discarding cards with graveyard value and casting creatures turns selection into a useful engine.
cards.watch: It is a small three-mana body and needs to survive summoning sickness before tapping; tokens do not untap it.

cards.name: Chandra, Chill of Compliance
cards.role: A flexible planeswalker for spell-heavy decks
cards.why: It can select cards, help cast noncreature spells or keep a threat tapped.
cards.better: A high density of noncreature, nonland cards improves the chance its surveil ability adds a card to hand.
cards.watch: Ordinary creature-heavy decks get less from the plus abilities, and stun counters consume loyalty.

cards.name: Fblthp, Impossibly Lost
cards.role: Conditional card draw from a small creature
cards.why: Dealing combat damage to an opponent can turn two mana into two cards.
cards.better: An available evasive attack lets you cast it before combat with a credible plan to trigger it.
cards.watch: Without a successful attack it is just a small body; the empty-library win is an exceptional outcome, not the normal plan.

cards.name: Geist of Saint Thalia
cards.role: A cost reducer for noncreature spells
cards.why: Repeated discounts can let you develop more spells in a turn.
cards.better: Several noncreature spells with generic mana in their costs give the ability meaningful work.
cards.watch: It cannot reduce coloured requirements, and a creature-heavy deck gets little beyond a small flyer.

cards.name: Hapatra, the Desert Frost
cards.role: A tempo creature that opens an attack
cards.why: Tapping and stunning an opposing creature creates a window for pressure.
cards.better: Use the window to attack life totals or a planeswalker while adding your own substantial creature.
cards.watch: The creature returns to action later; the untap ability also needs three mana.

cards.name: Jace, Reality Sculptor
cards.why: It can fuel a Jace token or suppress incoming combat damage for a turn.
cards.better: A blue-heavy deck with protection for its planeswalkers gets more from its loyalty abilities.
cards.watch: The defensive ability spends substantial loyalty, and twenty-five total loyalty is a demanding alternate finish.
cards.disagreement: Quinn is interested in the ultimate as a possible empower-deck win condition; Josh treats it as an unlikely bonus.

cards.name: Lyra, Tolarian Archangel
cards.role: A flyer with a draw-and-token ceiling
cards.why: Drawing three cards in one turn makes an Angel, and its activated ability can help reach that total.
cards.better: A clear flying attack and five spare mana can turn the normal draw plus two combat-damage draws into a token.
cards.watch: The activated ability still requires combat damage to a player; removal or a blocker can deny the payoff.

cards.name: Proft, Consulting Detective
cards.role: Selection that can become cards and counters
cards.why: Each scry or surveil offers a paid draw and a counter on an already useful early creature.
cards.better: Cheap recurring selection leaves enough mana to pay for its trigger.
cards.watch: The extra card costs two mana each time; budget for that on top of the enabling spell.

cards.name: Ruric Thar, Biomagus
cards.why: Double prowess makes noncreature spells threatening, and opposing targeted interaction draws you a card.
cards.better: A slower blue deck with enough early defence can use it to close the game.
cards.watch: Six mana does nothing for your early curve, and drawing a card does not prevent the removal spell from resolving.

cards.name: Samut, Tyrant of Naktamun
cards.role: A small creature with specialised spell protection
cards.why: Split second can stop ordinary responses while your instant or sorcery is on the stack.
cards.better: A spell-heavy plan facing counterspells or instant-speed protection gets more from the ability.
cards.watch: It does not improve the small body, and triggered abilities can still occur under split second.
cards.disagreement: Quinn sees too little payoff for a small creature; Josh values the baseline and occasional protected spell more highly.

cards.name: Tetsuko Umezawa, Fugitive
cards.role: Evasion for low-power or low-toughness creatures
cards.why: It makes qualifying creatures unblockable, including itself.
cards.better: Several creatures with power or toughness one or less are needed to make this a team payoff.
cards.watch: Counters and pumps can remove a creature's eligibility; check both current power and toughness.
cards.disagreement: Quinn is optimistic based on earlier formats; Josh doubts this set supplies enough suitable creatures.

cards.name: Traxos, Academy Guardian
cards.why: A noncreature spell first can make its flying, vigilant body cost only two mana.
cards.better: Cheap spells let you develop it while keeping mana for the rest of your turn.
cards.watch: Count the enabling spell's cost too; the discount does not mean every opening hand can play it on turn two.

cards.name: Way of the Cryomancer
cards.role: A planeswalker engine for copying spells
cards.why: It supplies loyalty and a way to copy a later instant or sorcery.
cards.better: Useful spells, more empower and protection for your planeswalker can build repeated value.
cards.watch: Activate before casting the spell you intend to copy; it uses that planeswalker's loyalty activation for the turn.

cards.name: Yargle, Goliath of Otaria
cards.why: Very high toughness blocks many ground threats and can protect a planeswalker.
cards.better: A defensive deck short of blockers, or a specific toughness payoff, has the clearest use for it.
cards.watch: Five mana buys no evasion, removal or arrival value; it does little to turn a stalled game into a win.

cards.name: Yuriko, Hope from the Shadows
cards.role: A cheap flash trick with a selection fallback
cards.why: It can shrink an attacker based on your graveyard or surveil to improve future draws.
cards.better: A stocked graveyard makes the combat mode effective, while selection payoffs reward the other mode.
cards.watch: The shrink scales with cards actually in your graveyard; an early empty graveyard offers no power reduction.

cards.name: Danitha, Spear of Agony
cards.role: A first-strike threat that needs targeted spells
cards.why: Spells aimed at an opponent or their creatures grow it before combat resolves.
cards.better: Cheap targeted removal and prepared damage spells can add counters while doing useful work.
cards.watch: A small starting body is weak without enough qualifying spells; abilities alone do not trigger it.

cards.name: Gallia, Tragic Host
cards.role: An early attacker with repeatable recursion
cards.why: Menace supplies pressure, and later it can return larger from the graveyard.
cards.better: Self-mill and spare creature cards in the graveyard make the return easier to support.
cards.watch: Each return costs five mana and another creature card, and it enters tapped; there is no finality counter limiting future returns.

cards.name: Gideon the Oathless
cards.role: A sticky threat with incidental damage
cards.why: Ward can make targeted removal cost another card, while opposing development slowly deals damage.
cards.better: An aggressive deck or noncombat-damage payoffs makes the extra points more relevant.
cards.watch: Ward does not stop untargeted removal or a larger blocker, and the opponent controls when the damage triggers occur.

cards.name: Liliana the Repentant
cards.role: A self-mill enabler with a one-time payoff
cards.why: Other creatures and planeswalkers repeatedly stock the graveyard, then exhaust can return a valuable card.
cards.better: Graveyard payoffs and a worthwhile reanimation target reward the setup.
cards.watch: The mill is mandatory, the activation costs six mana, and exhaust is normally usable only once for this permanent.

cards.name: Loot, the Anomaly
cards.role: A sacrifice payoff with unusual combat math
cards.why: At threshold it can sacrifice other creatures or planeswalkers to make its negative power deal more combat damage.
cards.better: A stocked graveyard and expendable permanents let it threaten extra damage after blocks.
cards.watch: Count the final power carefully: increasing a negative power toward zero reduces its combat damage.
cards.disagreement: Quinn rates the sacrifice outlet highly; Josh is much less convinced that the damage gain justifies feeding it permanents.

cards.name: Mabel, Bitter Recluse
cards.role: A cheap deathtouch blocker with counter removal
cards.why: The body can trade up, while removing counters sometimes weakens a creature or drains a planeswalker.
cards.better: Opposing loyalty or +1/+1 counters give the arrival trigger a valuable target.
cards.watch: Its baseline is still a 1/1, and the counter-removal bonus varies considerably by board.

cards.name: Massacre Girl, Most Wanted
cards.role: A growing threat that rewards deaths and damage
cards.why: Other friendly creatures or planeswalkers dying drain the opponent, and noncombat damage grows it.
cards.better: Sacrifice fodder and repeated damage sources can make it large quickly.
cards.watch: Five-mana slots are limited; without triggers it has to justify its place as a normal top-end creature.
cards.disagreement: Quinn is enthusiastic about the growing death-trigger engine; Josh wants a deck specifically able to exploit it.

cards.name: Proft, Sinister Mastermind
cards.role: A large threat locked behind threshold
cards.why: A very cheap large menace creature is the payoff for stocking your graveyard.
cards.better: Several self-mill sources make seven graveyard cards a realistic casting condition.
cards.watch: You cannot cast it below threshold; the discard mode only reduces toughness by one.

cards.name: Teyo, Diamondblade Mage
cards.role: A flash combat trick with a body
cards.why: Giving deathtouch and a counter can turn one of your creatures into a dangerous blocker or attacker.
cards.better: First strike makes the deathtouch especially effective, or it can target itself on entry.
cards.watch: Four mana is expensive for the base body, and the deathtouch lasts only for the turn.

cards.name: Tinybones, Pocket Nuisance
cards.why: The arrival trigger can take a card while developing your board and enabling noncombat-damage payoffs.
cards.better: Play it while the opponent has cards, with additional discard or cycling for later damage triggers.
cards.watch: The opponent chooses the discarded card, and an empty hand removes the main source of immediate value.

cards.name: Way of the Deathbringer
cards.role: Convert a small creature into a larger token
cards.why: The granted loyalty ability can upgrade expendable creatures to 4/4 tramplers.
cards.better: Small tokens or creatures whose arrival effects already paid off make suitable sacrifices.
cards.watch: It needs a creature as well as a planeswalker; you exchange a body rather than simply gaining another.

cards.name: Way of the Necromancer
cards.why: Creature deaths can replenish planeswalkers after the initial empower.
cards.better: A substantial sacrifice plan and a protected planeswalker are needed to keep generating value.
cards.watch: Both reviewers consider the setup excessive; two initial loyalty counters alone do not buy a Jace draw.

cards.name: Winter, Tormented Loner
cards.role: A flexible sacrifice effect and graveyard threat
cards.why: You can choose whether to exchange a permanent for an opposing sacrifice, or simply keep the growing creature.
cards.better: Expendable bodies and creature or planeswalker cards in your graveyard support both halves.
cards.watch: The opponent chooses their creature to sacrifice, and increasing Winter's power does not increase its toughness.
cards.disagreement: Quinn values the optional sacrifice and growing body; Josh sees a fragile creature and an unreliable removal exchange.

cards.name: Yargle, Glutton of Urborg
cards.why: It threatens substantial damage if it can connect.
cards.better: A specific way to exploit its power or force damage through is needed to justify it.
cards.watch: Five mana buys no evasion or arrival value, and three toughness makes it easy to trade with or remove.

cards.name: Ajani Unrelenting
cards.role: A planeswalker that builds an army while acting
cards.why: Every loyalty activation you make creates a Cadet, while its own abilities can sweep, pressure or refill.
cards.better: Other planeswalkers and existing tokens amplify its immediate and continuing value.
cards.watch: The sweep spares only tokens you control: it still damages opposing tokens and your nontoken creatures.

cards.name: Arni, Renowned Champion
cards.role: An attacker dependent on fresh creatures
cards.why: Other creatures entering temporarily add their power to its trampling body.
cards.better: A steady stream of creatures, especially large ones, creates threatening attacks.
cards.watch: Without an arrival trigger it has very little power; do not evaluate it only by its best attack.

cards.name: Gallia, the Merrymaker
cards.role: A hasty two-drop with counter support
cards.why: It attacks immediately and can give new creatures counters and haste.
cards.better: Creatures arriving with counters can use the haste without another payment.
cards.watch: Its own counter activation costs two mana and taps Gallia, so include that cost when planning an attack.

cards.name: Jiang Yanggu, Alone
cards.role: A five-drop rewarding a single attacker
cards.why: It improves a creature attacking a player alone while filtering a card.
cards.better: An evasive attacker or other discard earlier that turn increases the payoff.
cards.watch: It competes with stronger five-drops, and the single-attacker requirement can conflict with a wide aggressive board.

cards.name: Kiora of Fire and Ashes
cards.role: A flying payoff split across two bodies
cards.why: The Dragon provides immediate pressure while Kiora remains to make more later.
cards.better: Ramp helps reach six mana, and reusing the arrival effect can create another Dragon.
cards.watch: The repeat activation costs eight mana; value the first Dragon before assuming an endless supply.

cards.name: Koth, the Geomancer
cards.why: Every land triggers damage, and Mountains also add red mana.
cards.better: Damage payoffs use the trigger, while a timely Mountain can accelerate a larger play.
cards.watch: Only Mountains provide mana, and the mana is temporary: spend it in the same step or phase.

cards.name: Marwyn, the Clearcutter
cards.role: An early attacker that uses excess resources later
cards.why: A cheap body can pressure early, then turn spare lands or artifacts into fresh cards.
cards.better: Heartwoods or surplus lands make useful fuel once your mana needs are covered.
cards.watch: Sacrificing mana sources too soon can prevent you casting later draws; the activation also costs two mana and a tap.

cards.name: Pia, Determined Rebuilder
cards.role: Two bodies with a late mana sink
cards.why: The creature and flying Thopter supply useful value for three mana.
cards.better: Extra artifacts can make its expensive power boost a late-game threat.
cards.watch: The six-mana activation is a bonus; judge the card primarily by the two bodies it provides.

cards.name: Samut, Hazoret's Champion
cards.role: A two-drop that makes later threats immediate
cards.why: Team haste turns subsequent creatures into attacks without another setup cost.
cards.better: An aggressive creature deck takes the greatest advantage of the tempo.
cards.watch: Haste matters less when your creatures need to stay back and block.
cards.disagreement: Josh values team haste very highly; Quinn sees a useful upgrade on other hasty two-drops rather than a top priority.

cards.name: Tetsuko Umezawa, Pursuer
cards.role: A double-strike payoff for cheap spells
cards.why: Prowess increases damage in both combat-damage steps, with extra damage from some small blockers.
cards.better: Cheap noncreature spells make attacks hard to block safely.
cards.watch: It has no built-in evasion and leaves no extra value if removed before combat pays off.

cards.name: Tomik, Izzet Sparkmage
cards.why: Adding one to each noncombat-damage event can substantially improve repeated small pings.
cards.better: Many damage sources, including damage-based removal, give the static ability repeated work.
cards.watch: A deck with few suitable sources gets much less from its small body.
cards.disagreement: Quinn is optimistic about plentiful damage sources; Josh wants a particularly concentrated damage deck.

cards.name: Way of the Pyromancer
cards.role: Turn a planeswalker into a mana source
cards.why: The granted plus ability can provide red mana while building loyalty.
cards.better: A ramp plan with ways to protect the planeswalker gives the enchantment a purpose.
cards.watch: Using the mana ability consumes a loyalty activation; the initial two counters do not immediately buy a draw.
cards.disagreement: Quinn values an early ramp option; Josh thinks the enchantment's payoff is too small for a card.

cards.name: Way of the Warlord
cards.role: Turn loyalty into repeated small damage
cards.why: Its initial empower can fund damage to a threat and a player, with later empower enabling more shots.
cards.better: Small opposing creatures and noncombat-damage payoffs make the ability useful.
cards.watch: Two damage misses larger creatures, and you cannot also surveil with the same planeswalker that turn.

cards.name: Winter, Team Player
cards.role: A wide-board payoff for noncreature spells
cards.why: Convoke can help cast it and later spells boost your team's power.
cards.better: Token-producing spells help supply both the creature count and the noncreature-spell triggers.
cards.watch: The deck needs both bodies and spells; tapping attackers to convoke can delay the pressure.
cards.disagreement: Quinn expects it to be playable in the right curve; Josh is more sceptical about satisfying both requirements.

cards.name: Edgar, Moonlit Sovereign
cards.role: A flash threat with ways to grow
cards.why: A large surprise blocker can win a combat before its growth abilities matter.
cards.better: Holding mana for flash or activated abilities can leave your own turn spell-free for its end-step counters.
cards.watch: The growth check is at your end step and requires casting no spell that turn; casting Edgar on your turn prevents it.

cards.name: Fblthp, Knows the Way
cards.role: Land selection on a scalable creature
cards.why: It can find differently named basic lands to support future land drops and splashes.
cards.better: A green base using several basic land types makes both the search and its power more effective.
cards.watch: The lands go to hand, not the battlefield, and its power counts basic land types actually in play.

cards.name: Garruk, Curse Breaker
cards.role: A planeswalker with immediate board and card value
cards.why: Making a 4/4 also triggers its card draw, while its other abilities support mana or a decisive attack.
cards.better: Other four-power creatures provide more cards without spending loyalty.
cards.watch: Protect the remaining planeswalker after its first activation; each planeswalker still gets only one loyalty activation per turn.

cards.name: Ghalta the Unstoppable
cards.role: A discounted finisher that grants team trample
cards.why: A creature already on board reduces the cost of a large threat that helps damage get through.
cards.better: A reliable supply of large creatures makes the discount realistic.
cards.watch: An empty or diminished board can leave it close to its nine-mana starting cost.

cards.name: Jiang Yanggu, Never Alone
cards.why: Four mana provides both Jiang and Mowu, with an end-step untap for all your tokens.
cards.better: Attacking creature tokens and tapped Heartwoods make the untap especially useful.
cards.watch: Mowu is legendary, and the untap happens at your end step rather than immediately after attacking.

cards.name: Loot, the Nexus
cards.role: Ramp and fixing that scale with your board
cards.why: Different creature powers can produce several mana of one chosen colour.
cards.better: A varied board lets it accelerate large threats or cover multiple symbols of a splash colour.
cards.watch: Count distinct powers, not creatures; several creatures with the same power only contribute once.

cards.name: Marwyn, the Preserver
cards.role: An efficient body with land recovery
cards.why: A useful two-drop can turn milled lands into future land drops.
cards.better: Self-mill gives the activated ability reliable targets.
cards.watch: Returning a land costs two mana and puts it in hand; the hexproof clause is usually a minor bonus.

cards.name: Pia, Aether Ascetic
cards.role: Find a useful enchantment while developing a creature
cards.why: Discarding a card can turn its arrival into a search for a specific enchantment.
cards.better: Removal enchantments or a strong engine provide worthwhile targets, especially when the discarded card has graveyard value.
cards.watch: Without a useful enchantment in the library it is a modest body; the discard means the search is not extra card advantage.

cards.name: Ruric Thar, Magecrusher
cards.why: Reach, vigilance and trample let it attack while defending, with initial hexproof protecting the investment.
cards.better: Ramp and early defence help you reach seven mana.
cards.watch: Hexproof ends after it deals combat damage, including to a blocker; it does not require hitting a player.

cards.name: Titanbones, Towering Heart
cards.role: A lifegain payoff that grows quickly
cards.why: Each lifegain event adds two counters to a reach creature.
cards.better: Several reliable lifegain sources can turn it into a dominant blocker and attacker.
cards.watch: Without lifegain its body is underwhelming, and size alone does not get through repeated chump blocks.
cards.disagreement: Quinn rates it highly as a lifegain payoff; Josh wants particularly strong support before including it.

cards.name: Way of the Paradox
cards.role: Loyalty activations that support land drops
cards.why: It supplies loyalty, then rewards activations with life and permission to play another land.
cards.better: Spare lands in hand and lifegain payoffs give the continuing trigger useful work.
cards.watch: An extra land allowance does not find a land, and activating a planeswalker still requires timing and protection.
cards.disagreement: Quinn sees useful Explore-like value; Josh thinks the three-mana setup and conditional extras are insufficient.

cards.name: Way of the Wildspeaker
cards.role: A loyalty engine that makes large tokens
cards.why: Seven initial loyalty can fund a 4/4 trampler and leave fuel for a later turn.
cards.better: Further empower effects can repeatedly turn loyalty into meaningful board presence.
cards.watch: The remaining three loyalty cannot be cashed in on the same planeswalker's first turn after making the Beast.

cards.name: Edgar, Ancient Bloodlord
cards.role: A sacrifice outlet that grows and gains life
cards.why: Spare creatures or planeswalkers become lasting counters and temporary menace.
cards.better: Tokens or creatures whose arrival value is already spent make efficient fuel.
cards.watch: Each activation costs two mana and another permanent; keep resources needed for future turns.

cards.name: Hapatra, the Desert Fang
cards.role: A removal creature powered by the graveyard
cards.why: Its arrival can permanently shrink a creature based on the largest mana value in your graveyard.
cards.better: Self-mill and a costly card in the graveyard make it a strong two-for-one.
cards.watch: A nearly empty graveyard makes the removal weak; double black matters when considering a splash.

cards.name: Karn, Gilded Guardian
cards.role: A large artifact with conditional card draw
cards.why: Coloured artifacts can turn its arrival into several cards alongside a vigilant trampler.
cards.better: A Heartwood supplies red and green by itself, while other colours can increase the draw.
cards.watch: Count distinct colours, not artifacts. Its flexible symbols can still make it very expensive, and colourless artifacts add no cards.

cards.name: Kiora of Salt and Sand
cards.role: A planeswalker payoff with useful evasion
cards.why: Activating loyalty before attacking can make an attacker unblockable and untap it.
cards.better: Regular loyalty activations support the first ability without needing to reach eight loyalty.
cards.watch: Kiora does not supply empower itself; the eight-loyalty Leviathan is a demanding additional payoff.

cards.name: Mabel, Valley Hero
cards.role: Counters for a steady stream of creatures
cards.why: Every friendly creature entering supplies a counter for a creature that entered that turn.
cards.better: Token makers or multiple creatures in a turn offer more flexibility in placing the counters.
cards.watch: You cannot place the counter on an older creature just because it is your best attacker.

cards.name: Saheeli, Jewel of Avishkar
cards.why: Every noncreature spell creates a hasty Thopter, turning ordinary spells into board presence.
cards.better: Cheap spells let it produce several attackers in one turn.
cards.watch: It needs spells after it resolves; a hand already emptied of noncreature spells leaves little immediate value.

cards.name: Tam, the Possibility
cards.role: A specialised five-colour planeswalker support card
cards.why: Its abilities reward actual planeswalker spells and a wide variety of planeswalker types.
cards.better: An unusually well-fixed deck with several relevant planeswalkers would be needed to exploit it.
cards.watch: Empower does not cast a planeswalker spell, and the five-colour activation is unrealistic for most two-colour decks.

cards.name: Vraska, Soul of Stone
cards.why: Noncreature spells add vigilant artifact creatures that can later be spent for mana.
cards.better: A well-fixed spells deck can use the growing board and occasional mana conversion.
cards.watch: The tokens are creatures, so summoning sickness prevents immediately tapping them for mana without haste.

cards.name: Vraska, the Cutting Glare
cards.role: An efficient threat with a late removal mode
cards.why: Early it is a large deathtouch creature; with six lands its arrival also destroys an opposing permanent.
cards.better: A black-green base can cast it naturally and choose between early pressure and late value.
cards.watch: The six-land condition counts lands, not total mana sources, and the destroyed permanent's controller gets a Treasure.

cards.name: Karn, Argent Defender
cards.role: A sideboard tool against arrival triggers
cards.why: It shuts off abilities triggered by artifacts and creatures entering.
cards.better: An opponent relying heavily on those triggers provides the reason to bring it in.
cards.watch: The effect is symmetrical and can disable your own empower arrival triggers and other important enters abilities. Entering prepared is not a triggered ability.

cards.name: Traxos, Scourge Eternal
cards.role: A large trampler needing a continuing spell supply
cards.why: Its size is useful for four mana and creature or artifact spells untap it.
cards.better: A creature-heavy deck can keep it attacking and sometimes untap it after combat.
cards.watch: It does not untap normally; topdecking lands or nonartifact noncreature spells can leave it stuck.
cards.disagreement: Josh expects the untap requirement to be easy; Quinn gives the drawback more weight and mainly wants it where large bodies are scarce.
